title: The River That Forgot
subtitle: Water cycles · shared resources · connected systems
intro: The lighthouse has gone dark, and water no longer reaches the high gardens. Mira and Ivo must trace the old waterworks and restore four seals. The islands are imaginary; the clues use real ideas about water. Speak to the keepers, read each mechanism, and find out where a broken connection can change an entire system.
ending: The beacon glows. Water rises as vapour, condenses into droplets, returns as rain and gathers again. You have repaired the island’s connections and shared a limited supply according to the town’s needs. A cycle has many routes; this journey followed just one of them.

dialogue.quay: Aster: “Our spring feeds both the mill and the gardens. The beacon is not a pump; it is our signal that the four old mechanisms work. Start with the Memory Gate in Mossbell Woods. Restore any of the four seals in any order.”
dialogue.woods: Tala: “Watch the lake in sunlight. Liquid water can evaporate into water vapour. When the vapour cools, it can condense into droplets. Clouds hold droplets or ice crystals, not just invisible vapour. Follow a drop on one possible journey.”
dialogue.mill: Rook: “Today the river gives us eight measured units. The mill needs six to run safely and the town tank needs two. The sluice must share all eight. These are the needs of our imaginary machinery, not a general rule for real water systems.”
dialogue.quarry: Nim: “Some water soaks into the ground instead of running straight into rivers. Our simple gate shows only one route through a much larger cycle. The prism creature is restless; its weakness is gale magic.”
dialogue.forge: Jori: “Evaporation can happen below boiling temperature. Heat can increase it, but a puddle does not have to boil to dry. The cinder sentinel is vulnerable to tide magic. Guard before a heavy attack.”
dialogue.observatory: Edda: “Our demonstration has three stations. The first adds heat to help water evaporate. The second cools vapour so droplets form. The last collects the liquid. Set the lenses to those jobs.”
dialogue.archive: Sable: “Names are useful when they point to something you can observe. A drying wet cloth suggests evaporation; droplets on a cold surface can show condensation; falling rain is precipitation. Connect each description to its process.”
dialogue.beacon: Teacher: “You have followed a cycle, allocated a limited supply and connected processes to observations. Four seals will wake the Warden. Inspect it, use tide magic and guard when it prepares a crushing wave.”

sequence.title: A drop’s journey
sequence.prompt: Begin with sunlight on a lake. Arrange this simplified route until water gathers on the ground again. The real water cycle has many branching routes.
sequence.hint: Start with liquid becoming vapour. Cooling comes before rain.
sequence.explanation: On this route: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection. Water also travels by runoff, infiltration and other routes.

allocation.title: Share the current
allocation.prompt: Eight units arrive. The mill requires six units and the town tank requires two. Move the dividing gate; every unit must go somewhere.
allocation.hint: The two amounts must add to eight. Put six on the mill side.
allocation.explanation: 6 + 2 = 8. Allocation respects both the total available supply and the stated needs of this fictional system.

matching.title: Threads of water
matching.prompt: Connect each observation with its process.
matching.hint: Evaporation is liquid to vapour. Condensation forms droplets. Precipitation falls from clouds.
matching.explanation: The same water can move between places and states. These observations are examples of three different processes.
left: Droplets form on a cold mirror

dials.title: The three stations
dials.prompt: Set each station to its job: encourage evaporation, condense the vapour, then collect the liquid.
dials.hint: Add heat at the first station, cool the second, and store the liquid at the third.
dials.explanation: Heating can help evaporation; cooling vapour can produce condensation. The final station collects liquid rather than changing its state.
